cards.title: Does a constant margin force bounded sign-rank?
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every real ρ∈(0,1], does there exist a finite integer d(ρ), independent of matrix dimensions, such that every finite sign matrix A with margin m(A)≥ρ has sign-rank at most d(ρ)? This is the dimension-free bounding-function question written in the source as rank±(A)≤η(m(A)^{−1}); no polynomial or computable bound on η is requested.
cards.why: Asks whether robust high-dimensional point–halfspace representations can always be replaced by bounded-dimensional representations, connecting geometric learning parameters with communication complexity.
cards.status_note: The primary definitions and question were matched to the explicit open restatement in the March 2026 conference-version revision. April 2026 partial-matrix progress was checked separately. No total-matrix resolution was located through 12 September 2026.

references.title: Lower Bound Methods for Sign-Rank and Their Limitations
references.authors: Hatami, Hamed; Hatami, Pooya; Pires, William; Tao, Ran; Zhao, Rosie

cards.definitions: A sign matrix A∈{−1,+1}^{r×s} has positive finite numbers r,s of rows and columns and has every entry specified. Its sign-rank rank±(A) is the least D≥1 for which there are unit vectors u₁,…,uᵣ,v₁,…,vₛ∈ℝᴰ with Aᵢⱼ⟨uᵢ,vⱼ⟩>0 for all i,j. Equivalently it is the minimum real rank of a matrix B satisfying AᵢⱼBᵢⱼ>0 entrywise; zero entries do not realize either sign. The margin m(A) is the supremum, over such unit-vector representations in all finite dimensions D, of min_{i,j} Aᵢⱼ⟨uᵢ,vⱼ⟩. It lies in (0,1]. In optimizing margin, the representation dimension is unrestricted; the representation of least dimension need not maximize margin. The requested d may grow arbitrarily rapidly as ρ tends to zero, but for each fixed positive ρ it must bound all matrix sizes. Equivalently, one can use a finite nondecreasing bounding function η:[1,∞)→ℕ. This uniform bounded-margin interpretation is explicitly restated in the later source’s Open Problem 1.3. Matrices with missing or promise-restricted entries are excluded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a finite size-independent bound d(ρ) for every positive margin threshold ρ, or prove there is a fixed ρ>0 and a sequence of fully specified finite sign matrices with margins at least ρ and unbounded sign-ranks. No efficient procedure for producing the low-dimensional representation is required. Unbounded sign-rank with margins tending to zero, or only for partial matrices, does not refute the statement.

cards.title: Can a low-influence direction be removed from a convex set?
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a function τ:(0,1)→[0,1] with lim_{ε→0⁺}τ(ε)=0 such that the following holds for every n≥1, every centrally symmetric convex Borel set K⊆ℝⁿ, every unit vector v and every ε∈(0,1)? If Inf_v[K]≤ε, then there exists a centrally symmetric convex Borel set C⊆v⊥ such that γₙ(K △ (C+ℝv))≤τ(ε). The same τ must work in all dimensions and for all such sets and directions.
cards.why: Would make convex influence a robust measure of whether a Gaussian direction matters, strengthening the analogy between symmetric convex sets and Boolean functions with irrelevant variables.

references.title: Convex Influences
references.authors: De, Anindya; Nadimpalli, Shivam; Servedio, Rocco A.

cards.definitions: γₙ is standard Gaussian probability measure, the law of X with independent N(0,1) coordinates. Central symmetry means K=−K, with symmetry about the origin. Convexity means tx+(1−t)y∈K for x,y∈K and t∈[0,1]. Write 1_K for the indicator of K. The convex influence in a Euclidean unit direction v is Inf_v[K]=(1/√2) E[1_K(X)(1−⟨v,X⟩²)]. This is nonnegative for centrally symmetric convex K. The orthogonal subspace is v⊥={y:⟨v,y⟩=0}, and C+ℝv={y+tv:y∈C,t∈ℝ} is a cylinder whose membership depends only on the projection x−⟨v,x⟩v. The symmetric difference K△L consists of points in exactly one of K and L, so its Gaussian measure is the probability that their membership indicators disagree. Empty sets and the whole space are permitted. No lower or upper bound away from zero or one is imposed on γₙ(K), and no bound on total influence is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a single modulus τ tending to zero that bounds the Gaussian approximation error uniformly over the stated sets, dimensions and directions, or prove that no such modulus exists. Equivalently for a negative answer, exhibit a sequence with directional influence tending to zero while its Gaussian distance from every symmetric convex cylinder in that direction stays bounded below by a positive constant. A dimension-dependent modulus or a cylinder in some other direction does not suffice.

cards.title: Almost 3-colorable graphs versus graphs with no large independent set
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of constants 0<η<1 and 0<ε<(1−η)/3, is it NP-hard to distinguish graphs G on N vertices in which an induced subgraph on at least (1−η)N vertices is properly 3-colorable from graphs G with independence number α(G)<εN? This is the nonoverlapping promise range of the source’s Conjecture 23, whose intended demand is hardness for arbitrarily small positive η and ε.
cards.why: Would strengthen almost-coloring hardness enough to improve a central Vertex Cover approximation barrier, linking graph coloring promises with independent-set soundness.
cards.status_note: The full conjecture, its definition of induced coloring and the weaker proved theorem were checked. Subsequent-result searches through 12 September 2026, including the publisher abstract of the related MFCS 2025 matrix-completion paper, did not locate this stronger independent-set gap. That later abstract is not evidence of a resolution.

references.title: NP-Hardness of Almost Coloring Almost 3-Colorable Graphs
references.authors: Hecht, Yahli; Minzer, Dor; Safra, Muli

cards.definitions: G is a finite nonempty simple undirected graph, represented by its adjacency matrix or edge list. An independent set is a set of vertices containing no edge; α(G) is its maximum size. The subgraph induced by U⊆V(G) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in U. It is properly 3-colorable if a map U→{1,2,3} gives adjacent vertices different labels. Define iCol₃(G)=N^{−1}max{|U|:G[U] is 3-colorable}. The yes case is iCol₃(G)≥1−η, and the no case is α(G)/N<ε. Fractions refer to vertices, not edges or color classes of a fixed coloring. The parameters ε,η are fixed before the reduction and are not part of the graph input. In the usual deterministic NP-hardness formulation, for each pair there must be a deterministic polynomial-time map from Boolean satisfiability instances to graphs that sends satisfiable inputs into the yes case and unsatisfiable inputs into the no case. The polynomial may depend on ε and η. An algorithm for the promise problem may behave arbitrarily on graphs in neither case. Since a 3-colorable set has an independent subset of at least one third its size, the displayed parameter restriction ensures disjoint cases. The paper’s already proved weaker theorem allows randomized reductions; that distinction must be retained when assessing a claimed resolution.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated gap NP-hardness for every fixed admissible ε,η, with a reduction and its completeness and soundness guarantees, or refute the universal hardness assertion. If a claimed hardness result uses randomized reductions, state that convention explicitly and distinguish it from deterministic NP-hardness. A polynomial-time algorithm would contradict the deterministic hardness claim under P≠NP; without a complexity separation, it alone is not a logical refutation of NP-hardness.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
